title: Depth cues: overlap, size, placement, atmosphere, flat versus form
summary: Long before any vanishing point appears, a drawing already suggests depth through overlap, relative size, where things sit on the page, fading of distant values and whether a shape reads as flat or round. This module trains you to spot those cues in other people's work and to use them on purpose, so that later perspective construction has something to serve.
learning_outcomes: Name the main depth cues in any image and say which ones are doing the work
Turn a flat silhouette into something that reads as a solid form using overlap and contour
Push objects back in space with size, placement and reduced contrast and detail
Plan a simple image in foreground, middle ground and background planes

practice.title: One cue at a time thumbnails
practice.description: Draw three simple shapes (for example a hill, a tree and a building) six times at postage-stamp size. In each thumbnail use only one cue to separate them: overlap, size, vertical placement, value fade, detail fade, or a combination of two. Label which cue each uses.

practice.title: Layer map of a master
practice.description: Pick three Met Open Access prints. For each, make a 5-minute thumbnail that marks foreground, middle and background as separate value patches, then write one line naming the cues responsible for the depth.

practice.title: Flat to form
practice.description: Draw ten flat shapes (circles, squares, blobs). Turn each into a form by adding overlap, a visible back edge or contour lines wrapping around it, then draw a flat version beside it for comparison.

practice.title: Atmospheric ladder
practice.description: Draw a landscape with five receding hill or tree layers using at most four values. Lighten and simplify each layer as it recedes, and keep the nearest layer the darkest and most detailed.

practice.title: Photo overlap audit
practice.description: Choose five street or landscape photos. Trace only the places where one object overlaps another, in ink, and ignore everything else. Notice how much depth survives with just those junctions.

done_when: I can look at a picture and name which depth cues are carrying the space
A three-plane thumbnail reads as deep with no perspective lines at all
I can draw the same object so that it looks flat, then so that it looks round, on request
I can reduce contrast and detail in distant areas deliberately, rather than greying everything
common_mistakes: Relying on size alone and avoiding overlap, so objects float side by side
Letting edges of shapes just touch (tangents), which flattens the space
Fading the whole image evenly instead of lightening and simplifying only the distance
Treating higher on the page as always farther away, even when the object is above the horizon

title: The box: drawing a convincing rectangular form
summary: The box is the unit that nearly every later construction is built from. You learn to draw one so that its parallel edges converge consistently, its faces stay flat and it feels like a solid object rather than a wireframe. Volume of deliberate practice matters more than theory here.
learning_outcomes: Draw a box with confident, straight, single-stroke edges
Make the edges of each direction converge toward one shared point
Show hidden edges and overlap so the box reads as solid
Check your own box by extending its edges and seeing where they meet

practice.title: Line control warmup
practice.description: Fill a page with straight lines drawn from the shoulder in one stroke, using a ghosting motion (practise the stroke in the air before touching the paper). Aim for confident lines, not perfect ones.

practice.title: Extend-the-edges check
practice.description: Draw ten loose boxes, then extend every edge in a different colour and mark where each set of four lines meets. Circle the boxes where a set of edges fails to meet cleanly.

practice.title: Desk-object boxes
practice.description: Draw five real box-shaped objects (cereal packet, tissue box, book) from three viewpoints each. Look first, then draw: do not copy outlines, construct the edges.

practice.title: Overlap and stacking
practice.description: Draw clusters of three boxes of different sizes that overlap or touch, showing every hidden edge as a lighter line. Check that each box still has consistent convergence.

practice.title: Line weight pass
practice.description: Re-draw three of your best boxes and strengthen only the near corner and its three edges, leaving the far edges light. Compare to the unweighted versions.

done_when: Extended edges of a box meet close to a common point for each direction, with only small misses
My boxes stop flipping between two readings (the box-seen-from-above versus from-below flip)
I can draw a box from any of three clearly different views without a reference
My lines are single confident strokes, not scratchy repeats
common_mistakes: Drawing the far end of a box with edges that diverge, or with nearly parallel edges when they should converge visibly
Making boxes very deep and thin because the depth edges are drawn too long
Scratchy, repeated lines instead of a planned stroke from the shoulder
Moving on without extending edges to check, so the same error is repeated for months

title: Orthographic and isometric views: the bridge to 3D thinking
summary: Plans, elevations and isometric views show a form without perspective distortion and train you to hold a three-dimensional shape in mind. Architecture schools often teach this before perspective; it is also the language of 3D software viewports and spatial reasoning tests.
learning_outcomes: Draw front, top and side views of a simple object that agree with each other
Build an isometric drawing from those three views
Explain how parallel projection differs from perspective
Switch between orthographic and perspective views in a 3D tool

practice.title: Three views of everyday objects
practice.description: Draw front, top and side views of three small objects (stapler, mug, remote). Check that heights, widths and depths agree across the views.

practice.title: Isometric from three views
practice.description: Using one of your three-view sets, build an isometric drawing with 30-degree axes, then compare to the real object.

practice.title: Model and compare
practice.description: Build the same object in a free 3D tool from boxes and cylinders, view it in orthographic mode from front, top and side, and compare with your drawings.

practice.title: Convert to perspective
practice.description: Take your isometric drawing and redraw the same object in two-point perspective from a chosen horizon height.

practice.title: Snap-cube recall
practice.description: Build a small shape from toy cubes or blocks, hide it, and draw it in isometric from memory, then compare.

done_when: My three views of an object agree with each other
I can draw an isometric cube and a few stacked blocks with consistent axes
I can say what changes when you switch from orthographic to perspective in a 3D tool
I can turn a small block stack into either an isometric or a two-point perspective drawing
common_mistakes: Converging lines in an isometric drawing that should be parallel
Mixing scales between front, top and side views
Treating isometric as a cheap perspective and then being confused when scale does not shrink
Skipping the real or 3D object and trying to imagine everything

title: Horizon line, eye level, vanishing points and convergence
summary: The horizon is your eye level, and every set of parallel lines that runs away from you aims at a vanishing point. This module makes those facts physical: you find them in photographs, move them on purpose, and see what changes. It is the vocabulary the later one-, two- and three-point modules assume.
learning_outcomes: Explain why the horizon line equals eye level and where vanishing points sit
Find the horizon and vanishing points in a photograph
Predict whether a box's top face shows from above or below the horizon
Describe the picture plane and the viewer's position in plain words

practice.title: Horizon hunt
practice.description: Take ten photos (yours or from Unsplash) of streets, rooms and landscapes. On a printout or tracing layer, draw the horizon line and mark where it cuts through any standing people. Note when the horizon is above or below the middle of the frame.

practice.title: Same boxes, three horizons
practice.description: Draw the same group of three boxes with the horizon near the top of the page, in the middle, and near the bottom. Watch which faces appear and disappear.

practice.title: Find the vanishing points
practice.description: Take three photos of corridors, streets or buildings. Extend the converging lines to find each vanishing point, using a ruler on a printout or a vanishing-point guide in Krita.

practice.title: Receding posts
practice.description: Draw a ground plane with a row of identical posts running to a vanishing point on the horizon. Repeat with the horizon lowered and then raised and see how the tops of the posts behave.

practice.title: One-page explainer in your own words
practice.description: Write and sketch a one-page explanation of horizon, eye level, vanishing point and picture plane for someone who has never studied perspective. Re-read it a week later and fix what is vague.

done_when: Given any photo I can place the horizon and at least one vanishing point within a reasonable margin
I can state whether a horizontal surface will show its top or underside before drawing it
I never give two objects on the same ground plane different horizon lines
I can say what the picture plane is and why it sits between me and the subject
common_mistakes: Placing vanishing points off the horizon, or putting each object on its own horizon
Treating the top of distant hills or trees as the true horizon line
Putting vanishing points so close together that the result looks distorted when that was not the intent
Memorising the rules without testing them on photographs

title: One-point perspective: rooms, streets, squares and grids
summary: One-point perspective is the simplest system: one face of every box is parallel to you and every depth line runs to one vanishing point. You use it to build interiors, corridors, street scenes, floor grids and the rules for how equal steps shrink with distance.
learning_outcomes: Construct a one-point room or street with correct depth spacing
Draw a true square and a tile floor in one-point perspective
Place boxes and simple furniture on a grid of tiles
Recognise when a scene can and cannot be treated as one-point

practice.description: Draw a one-point room three times: with the vanishing point left of centre, central and right of centre. Add a doorway, a window and a floor line each time.

practice.title: Tile floor and diagonals

practice.title: Street canyon
practice.description: Draw a street between two rows of buildings with a pavement edge, receding windows and a row of lamp posts. Make the spacing of windows shrink with distance.

practice.title: Grid-assisted interior

practice.title: Photo recreations

done_when: I can set up a one-point room with a horizon, vanishing point and back wall in about two minutes
My tile floor rows get closer together toward the horizon rather than being evenly spaced
Front faces of my boxes stay square-on to me and their depth edges meet at the vanishing point
I can say when a scene needs two points because nothing is facing me squarely
common_mistakes: Spacing receding tiles or windows evenly instead of letting them compress
Tilting vertical lines while the depth lines converge
Leaving every scene at a centred vanishing point so the composition looks static
Using one-point for a box that is actually turned, which makes its front face lopsided

Explain how the two vanishing points move when a box is rotated
Draw an exterior corner and an interior corner

practice.title: Tilting box sequence
practice.description: Draw one box six times, tilting the view gradually from level to steeply upward. Mark the third vanishing point each time and note where the verticals begin to lean.

practice.title: City block from above
practice.description: Draw a bird's-eye block with four buildings of different heights, a street and two vehicle blocks. Keep every vertical aimed at one point below the scene.

practice.title: Ceiling view interior

practice.title: Grid helper

done_when: I know whether verticals should converge up or down for a given view
Verticals of all buildings in a scene share one third point rather than being parallel in some and converging in others
I can choose a moderate third point that gives a natural look rather than a dramatic one when I need it
I can sketch a plausible bird's-eye block without construction after practising with it
common_mistakes: Keeping verticals parallel while the other edges converge, producing an odd hybrid
Placing the third point too close to the horizon so the form collapses
Converging verticals toward the wrong side (bird's eye converges downward)
Forgetting that a horizon far above or below the subject is implied by a steep tilt

title: Ellipses in perspective: cylinders, cones, spheres and how they sit in boxes

learning_outcomes: Draw smooth ellipses of any openness with a confident arm motion
Align an ellipse's minor axis with the axis of its cylinder
Judge how open each end of a cylinder should be from its distance to eye level
Fit a cylinder, cone or sphere inside a box and draw it consistent with the box

practice.title: Cylinder stack
practice.description: Draw a tall cylinder with its axis marked, then add rings at five heights. Show how rings above eye level open downward and rings below open upward, and the ring at eye level collapses to a line.

practice.title: Cone and sphere in a box
practice.description: Draw a cube and fit a cone with its base on the floor face, then a separate cube with a sphere touching all six faces. Mark contact points.

practice.title: Real cylinders
practice.description: Draw five real cylinders (tin, mug, roll of tape, bottle, pencil pot) with the minor axis line drawn first. Compare ellipse openness at top and base.

practice.title: Wheel on a wall
practice.description: Draw a wheel mounted on a side of a two-point box, then draw the same wheel on the opposite side. Notice that the ellipse's axis points to the same vanishing point as the box's depth edges.

done_when: My ellipses have rounded ends and no pointed tips or flat sides
The minor axis of an ellipse lines up with the object's axis
Ends of a cylinder differ in openness in the right direction relative to the horizon
I can place a sphere or cone in a box without checking each time
common_mistakes: Pointed or egg-shaped ellipses from short, hesitant strokes
Tilting the ellipse axis off the cylinder axis
Making the near and far ends of a cylinder equally open
Using the same ellipse shape for every circle in a scene regardless of its angle to the viewer

practice.title: Intersection pairs
practice.description: Draw fifteen pairs of simple forms that overlap (box with cylinder, sphere with box, cone with cylinder, two cylinders crossing). In each, draw the intersection curve as a line wrapping across both forms.

practice.title: Additive builds
practice.description: Choose five small household objects (kettle, toaster, desk lamp, mug, stapler). Draw each as stacked and joined primitives, transparent, with a short list of the primitives written beside it.

practice.title: Subtractive builds
practice.description: Start from a box or cylinder and carve it: a notch, a hole, a bevel, a slot. Draw six variations, then model two of them in Blender with a difference Boolean and compare.

practice.title: Product teardown
practice.description: Find three product photos on a free photo site. For each, write the list of primitives, draw the object transparent, then redraw it from a second viewpoint using only your construction.

practice.title: Hard-surface blockout

I can show a cut-away or notch and still have the remaining solid read as one form
I can redraw an object from a second angle using only my transparent construction

Putting an intersection line in only one of the two forms

Overlapping forms show which is in front without needing outlines
I can foreshorten an arm or leg without losing its volume
I exaggerate near forms enough that they read
common_mistakes: Drawing the long axis of a form at its full length when it points toward the viewer
Using flat cross-section lines instead of open ellipses on foreshortened limbs
Under-scaling the nearest part so the pose reads flat
Drawing the outline first and then trying to fix proportions, instead of constructing

school_reference.institution: Proko online atelier (The Perspective Course outline)

title: Shadows in perspective: cast shadows from the sun and from point lights
summary: A cast shadow has its own construction: lines from the light through an object's corners meet lines from a shadow vanishing point on the ground. You learn the method for a point light and for the sun, how shadows land on different surfaces, and how to check your result against a lit 3D scene.
learning_outcomes: Construct the cast shadow of a box from a point light
Adapt the method to sunlight and to different sun directions
Cast the shadow of a sphere or cylinder
Describe why shadow lengths change with the light's height

resources.title: Studio Chalkboard: Shadow Perspective (lesson 11)
resources.free_notes: Open web page, no login. No licence statement found. Page text does not name the author; authorship is taken from the site index.
resources.notes: Read the whole page and redraw the diagrams. Key ideas on the page: a vertical drop from the light finds the shadow vanishing point on the receiving surface, and for the sun the shadow point sits on the horizon below it.

resources.title: Drawing and Painting Cast Shadows Using Perspective
resources.free_notes: Article and embedded YouTube video are freely readable. The site also sells paid courses; this page is not one of them.
resources.notes: Matt Fussell's article and video: a box in two-point with a point light, a method for a sphere's elliptical shadow, and the note that a light close to the horizon casts longer shadows. Watch the video, then read the steps.

resources.title: The Theory and Practice of Perspective (1910)
resources.credit: G. A. Storey, teacher of perspective at the Royal Academy; Clarendon Press, Oxford
resources.free_notes: Gutenberg lists it as public domain in the USA (EPUB, Kindle, text, HTML). Storey died in 1919, so it should also be out of copyright in life-plus-70 countries such as Australia (my inference, not stated by Gutenberg).
resources.notes: Book IV, 'Shadow and Reflection', covers cast shadows from the sun and from artificial light, with a short section on reflections. Use for rigorous diagrams.

resources.title: Blender manual: Light Objects (point and sun lights)
resources.free_notes: Page title confirmed; body text did not come through my fetch, so I am relying on general knowledge that Blender offers point and sun lights.
resources.notes: Use the manual page for how Blender defines its light types, then place a box on a plane under a sun lamp and a point lamp and orbit the camera to check your drawn shadows.

practice.title: Point-light shadows
practice.description: Draw a box and mark a lamp above it. Construct the cast shadow from the light and a point beneath it. Repeat with the lamp moved higher, lower and to the other side.

practice.title: Three sun directions
practice.description: Draw the same box lit by the sun from the side, from behind you and from in front, using the sun method from the shadow page. Notice how the shadow lines behave in each case.

practice.title: Sphere and cylinder shadows
practice.description: Cast the shadow of a sphere and a cylinder using the box-around-the-form approach from the Virtual Instructor page.

practice.title: Shadow on two surfaces
practice.description: Draw an object on a tabletop near a wall, so the shadow falls on the table and then climbs the wall.

practice.title: Orbit check
practice.description: Reproduce one of your drawn setups in Blender with the same light type, then compare the shadow shape with what you drew.

done_when: I can construct a box shadow from a point light in a few minutes
I know which setups give a shadow vanishing point on the horizon and which give one on the ground
I can explain why a low light or low sun gives longer shadows
My shadows connect to the base of the object rather than floating
common_mistakes: Drawing shadow edges parallel on the page when they should converge
Starting the construction at the wrong corners of the box
Using the same shadow point for shadows on different surfaces
Forgetting to sketch the hidden back corners, so the shadow outline is wrong

title: Slopes, ramps, roofs, stairs and hills
summary: Inclined planes do not use the horizon for their vanishing points: roof pitches, ramps and downhill streets get points above or below it, on a vertical line through the flat-ground point. You learn the construction, then apply it to roofs, stairs and hillside streets.
learning_outcomes: Place an inclined vanishing point above or below the horizon for a rising or falling line
Draw a gabled roof and a ramp in two-point perspective
Space steps in a staircase correctly as they recede
Draw a street running up or down a hill without breaking the horizon

resources.notes: Lesson 10, 'Inclines: finding roof pitches and declines'. Read after the two-point lessons.

resources.title: Blender 5.2 LTS (free 3D software for checking your construction)
resources.free_notes: blender.org states Blender is free and open source under the GPL and may be used for any purpose. 5.2 LTS shows an initial release of 14 July 2026 and support to July 2028.
resources.notes: Build a ramp and a flight of stairs from boxes, orbit the camera, and see how the incline lines aim at points off the horizon.

practice.title: Gabled roof
practice.description: Draw a house in two-point with a gabled roof. Find the vanishing point for the roof edges and check that the ridge line is parallel to the walls' top edge in 3D.

practice.title: Ramp up and ramp down
practice.description: Draw a ramp rising away from you and another falling away from you, in the same ground plane. Mark where each set of slope lines meets.

practice.title: Staircase
practice.description: Draw a flight of eight steps going up and away. Make the step heights and depths shrink with distance, then draw the same stairs going down.

practice.title: Hillside street
practice.description: Draw a street running up a hill with houses on both sides. Keep the true horizon in view and mark it before you place the street's vanishing point.

practice.title: Blender comparison
practice.description: Model your stair or ramp in Blender from boxes, orbit to match your viewpoint, and compare incline lines.

done_when: I put sloped lines on a vanishing point above or below the horizon, on the right vertical
Steps and roof pitches look consistent in 3D from more than one viewpoint
I do not confuse the top of a hill with the true horizon
I can explain in a sentence why a ramp's vanishing point is not on the horizon
common_mistakes: Using the flat-ground vanishing point for sloped lines
Putting the sloped vanishing point off the vertical line through the flat-ground point
Spacing steps evenly down a staircase on the page
Raising the horizon to the top of a hill

title: Curvilinear, fisheye and extreme wide-angle perspective
summary: Straight-line perspective breaks down toward the edges of a very wide view; curvilinear systems bend straight lines into arcs to keep the whole view in one drawing. You learn the five-point layout, how fisheye differs from an ordinary wide angle, and how to use drawing-software helpers to keep your curves honest.
learning_outcomes: Describe five-point perspective: four points on a circle plus one at the centre
Know which lines stay straight in a fisheye drawing and which curve
Construct a simple fisheye room or street using a guide
Choose between ordinary wide angle and fisheye for a given picture

resources.title: Wikipedia: Curvilinear perspective (five-point, fisheye)
resources.free_notes: Free encyclopedia article. It describes five-point perspective as four vanishing points on a circle plus one at its centre, codified by Barre and Flocon in 1968.
resources.notes: Read for the definition, the five-point layout, and the history from van Eyck's Arnolfini Portrait through Escher to Barre and Flocon's 1968 book. It is a concept article, not a drawing lesson.

resources.title: Krita manual: Painting with Assistants (vanishing point, perspective, 2-point, fish-eye, curvilinear, ellipse)
resources.free_notes: Krita describes itself as a free and open source painting program on krita.org. The manual lists Vanishing Point, Perspective, 2 Point Perspective, Ruler and Parallel Ruler, Fish Eye Point, Perspective Ellipse and a Curvilinear Perspective assistant added in Krita 5.3.
resources.notes: Use the Fish Eye Point assistant and the Curvilinear Perspective assistant (added in Krita 5.3) to try curved guides on a digital canvas, and compare them against hand-drawn arcs.

resources.notes: Spanish workshop outline that lists conical and fisheye perspective, and mixing perspective with organic forms, as advanced exits from the three standard systems.

practice.title: Five-point grid by hand
practice.description: Draw a circle and mark four points on its rim at the compass points plus one at its centre. Then draw curved lines from each rim point through the circle to build a grid. Compare your grid against the desktop grid maker's 5-point setting.

practice.title: Fisheye room
practice.description: Draw a simple room as seen with a fisheye lens, with the centre lines straight and the others curved. Add a table and a window.

practice.title: Cube at the centre and at the edge
practice.description: Draw a cube in the middle of a fisheye grid and another near the border. Note how the straight edges bend near the border.

practice.title: Digital guide comparison
practice.description: Draw a street scene using a curvilinear guide in Krita, then redraw it by hand without the guide.

practice.title: Lens decision sheet
practice.description: Draw the same simple room three ways: normal view, wide angle and fisheye. Write two lines on what each one makes the viewer feel.

done_when: I can lay out a five-point grid without a template
I know which lines stay straight in fisheye and why
My curves meet their vanishing points instead of floating as arbitrary arcs
I can say when ordinary perspective is the better choice
common_mistakes: Curving every line by the same amount instead of in proportion to its distance from the centre
Curving lines that pass through the view centre, which should stay straight
Confusing a fisheye image with a plain wide-angle one
Using fisheye for a scene that does not need it, so the drawing looks gimmicky

school_reference.institution: UNAM Facultad de Artes y Diseno (workshop outline, Spanish)
school_reference.note: Outline runs: definitions and light and shadow, one-point, two-point, three-point, then fisheye and mixing perspective with organic forms.

title: Putting perspective together: a full scene with figures, repeats and shadows
summary: Combine everything: choose a horizon and viewpoint, build a grid, place buildings, objects and people at consistent scale, add repeating elements and cast shadows, and make composition decisions about which perspective to use. The goal is three finished scenes, each critiqued against its own construction.
learning_outcomes: Plan a scene on a thumbnail with horizon, vanishing points and focal area
Build the scene's space with a grid and place objects and people at believable scale
Add cast shadows and atmosphere that agree with the construction
Critique your own work by overlaying the construction and finding errors

practice.title: Scene planning thumbnails
practice.description: Before each project, draw six tiny thumbnails with different horizons, vanishing points and camera heights, and choose the one that best supports what the picture is about.

practice.title: One-point interior with figures
practice.description: Draw a one-point room with furniture and three same-height figures at different distances, with cast shadows from a window.

practice.title: Two-point street corner
practice.description: Draw a street corner with repeating windows, a staircase, a lamp post and its shadow, and several figures at consistent scale.

practice.title: Three-point bird's-eye plaza
practice.description: Draw a plaza from above with buildings of varied height, steps, and people as small marks that follow the horizon rule.

practice.title: Self-critique overlay
practice.description: After each drawing, extend its main lines on a copy and write 150 words naming three construction errors and what you would change. Redraw one corner of the picture to fix an error.

done_when: Three finished scenes (one-, two- and three-point) with construction visible beneath or beside them
People and repeated elements are consistent in scale across each scene
Cast shadows agree with the stated light
I can find at least three construction errors in my own finished work and say how to correct them
common_mistakes: Skipping the thumbnail stage and discovering the wrong viewpoint after hours of work
Rendering details before the construction is finished
Using the same horizon height for every scene
Never overlaying lines on finished work, so errors are never found

title: Drawing from imagination: rotating and combining forms, and building a visual library
summary: Invented drawings run on two things: a stock of structures you understand well enough to rebuild from memory, and the ability to rotate and combine them in perspective. This module is a long-term practice plan, not a single lesson: build a library from careful studies, test it with recall, then combine.
learning_outcomes: Study a subject until you can rebuild its structure from memory
Rotate a remembered object to a new viewpoint without a reference
Combine two or more remembered forms into an invented object or scene
Keep a small, organised library of references and studies to draw on

practice.title: Weekly subject library
practice.description: Pick one category each week (for example chairs, boots or street lamps). Collect ten photos from a free photo site, make three construction studies, and keep them in one folder.

practice.title: Study, then recall
practice.description: The day after studying an object, draw it from memory in a new viewpoint, then check against the reference and note which parts failed.

practice.title: Two-object fusion
practice.description: Choose two remembered objects (a kettle and a boot) and combine them into one invented object using shared primitives, drawn from two viewpoints.

practice.title: Primitive-only invention
practice.description: Draw ten invented objects from three primitives each, in perspective, with hidden edges.

practice.title: Blender scaffold
practice.description: Block out an invented scene with simple shapes in Blender, choose a camera, then draw the scene in a different viewpoint without looking at the model and check afterwards.

practice.title: Master study for structure
practice.description: Choose a print from the Met collection with strong spatial structure. Draw only its construction (horizon, forms, vanishing points), not its surface.

done_when: I have a folder of studied subjects and can rebuild several from memory
I can draw a studied object from a viewpoint I have never seen it from
My invented objects keep a consistent horizon and vanishing points
I can tell the difference between recalling a structure and merely copying a memorised outline
common_mistakes: Copying one reference outline instead of studying the structure under it
Starting from imagination before the construction skills are steady
Never checking recall against a reference
Studying only one familiar viewpoint of each subject
